power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional psychoeducation for bipolar disorder by grounding clinical content in the neural mechanisms underlying the illness.

This chapter reviews the neuroscience foundation relevant to bipolar disorder, including prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction, reward processing abnormalities that shift between mood states, circadian rhythm disruption, autonomic dysregulation, and the neuroplastic changes linked to illness progression and recovery.

We translate these mechanisms into accessible psychoeducational content addressing diagnosis, pathogenesis, risk factors, and treatment, and describe brain-based strategies spanning cognitive monitoring, circadian-focused interventions, and emerging digital phenotyping tools.
Delivery considerations are addressed with attention to the state-dependent nature of insight and cognitive function across mood episodes, phenotype-specific personalization, and family involvement.
We outline mechanisms through which NIPE may improve outcomes, including enhanced awareness, reduced stigma, improved treatment adherence, and greater selfefficacy.

While empirical evaluation of NIPE specifically for bipolar disorder remains limited, the chapter identifies priorities for future research, including randomized trials, mechanistic mediation analyses, and precision medicine approaches tailored to bipolar phenotype and illness course.

text.text: For individuals with bipolar disorder (BD), achieving and maintaining self-awareness presents unique challenges that distinguish this condition from other psychiatric disorders.

BD, characterized by recurrent episodes of mania or hypomania and depression, affects approximately 1-2% of the global population and is associated with substantial functional impairment, elevated suicide risk, and diminished quality of life (Merikangas, Jin et al. 2011) The challenges of impaired self-awareness in BD are multifaceted and statedependent.

text.text: This chapter provides a comprehensive examination of NIPE specifically designed for BD.
We first discuss neuroscientific principles in the context of BD, followed by an exploration of tailored strategies, delivery considerations, efficacy mechanisms, and future research directions.
By clarifying neural processes underlying BD and supporting development of personalized strategies, NIPE has potential to meaningfully enhance recovery trajectories.

The Principles of Neuroscience in BD 2.1 Neural Circuitry and Systems-Level Dysfunction BD is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of neural circuits, with particular emphasis on networks involved in emotion regulation, reward processing, and circadian rhythm maintenance (Liloia, Rocca et al. 2026).

text.text: Explaining these circuit-level changes to patients gives a physical basis for symptoms that otherwise feel like personal failures of control, and it sets up the specific compensatory strategies discussed in Section 4.
Emotion Regulation Networks: The prefrontal cortex, particularly the ventrolateral and dorsolateral regions, exerts top-down regulatory control over the amygdala, which processes emotional salience.

In BD, neuroimaging studies demonstrate reduced prefrontal activation and increased amygdala reactivity during emotional processing, suggesting impaired regulatory control (Steardo, D'Angelo et al. 2025).

In BD, both structural and functional ACC abnormalities contribute to difficulties in detecting and resolving emotional conflicts (Ogłodek, Vober et al. 2026).

text.text: Reward Processing Abnormalities: BD involves fundamental alterations in reward circuits involving the ventral striatum and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
Individuals show heightened striatal activation during manic phases, explaining increased goal-directed activity and risk-taking (Chen, Wang et al. 2022).

text.text: These cyclical alterations (i.e., oscillating between hyperactivation and hypoactivation) represent a core neurobiological feature distinguishing bipolar from unipolar depression.
Circadian Rhythm Dysregulation: The circadian system, orchestrated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, regulates 24-hour oscillations of sleep-wake cycles, hormones, and mood.
Individuals with BD show alterations in clock gene expression, melatonin patterns, and circadian amplitude (Campbell, Frye et al. 2025).

text.text: Clinically, episodes increase in frequency over time.
At the neural level, kindling involves long-term potentiation-like mechanisms in emotion circuits.
However, neuroplastic capacity offers opportunities for adaptive reorganization.
Lithium enhances neuroplasticity by increasing gray matter volume, promoting neurogenesis, and protecting against excitotoxic damage (Machado-Vieira, Soeiro-De-Souza et al. 2014).

Autonomic signals are also the most directly measurable of these systems, making them a practical entry point for the digital phenotyping strategies described in Section 4.3.
Beyond central nervous system alterations, BD involves significant autonomic dysfunction.

Heart rate variability (HRV), reflecting autonomic flexibility, is reduced in BD throughout different phases of the illness, including euthymia (Faurholt-Jepsen, Brage et al. 2017 , Faurholt-Jepsen, Kessing et al. 2017 , Ortiz, Bradler et al. 2021).

In BD, this coupling may become dysregulated, contributing to a disconnect between physiological arousal and subjective experience.

NIPE IN BD
Translating diagnostic criteria into brain-based language changes how symptoms are experienced, replacing self-blame with a mechanistic explanation patients can act on.

Brain-Based Explanations: Manic episodes can be explained as states where reward circuits become hyperactivated, dopamine signaling increases, and prefrontal regulatory control diminishes (Chen, Wang et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Brain-Based Explanations: Manic episodes can be explained as states where reward circuits become hyperactivated, dopamine signaling increases, and prefrontal regulatory control diminishes <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen, Wang et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, symptoms such as elevated mood arise from reward system overactivation; racing thoughts from accelerated processing with reduced filtering; impulsivity from weakened prefrontal inhibition; and reduced need for sleep from arousal system override.
A useful metaphor compares the manic brain to a car with stuck accelerator and failing brakes: the reward system overactivates while prefrontal cortex cannot effectively slow things down.

Conversely, depressive episodes involve hypoactive reward systems reducing pleasure capacity, reduced prefrontal cortex activity contributing to concentration difficulties, and overactive regions processing negative emotion fueling rumination (Steardo, D'Angelo et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Conversely, depressive episodes involve hypoactive reward systems reducing pleasure capacity, reduced prefrontal cortex activity contributing to concentration difficulties, and overactive regions processing negative emotion fueling rumination <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Steardo, D'Angelo et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: NIPE should emphasize that during depression, the brain has a negativity bias coloring perceptions, which is a cognitive distortion arising from altered neural processing.

Mixed Episodes: Mixed states, simultaneous depressive and manic symptoms, can be conceptualized as simultaneous activation of typically opposing systems: reward circuits may be hyperactive (producing agitation) while pleasure circuits are hypoactive (producing anhedonia).
NIPE content should validate these experiences as reflecting genuine neural complexity and note that mixed states carry particularly elevated suicide risk (Bartoli, Crocamo et al. 2020).
text.formatted: NIPE content should validate these experiences as reflecting genuine neural complexity and note that mixed states carry particularly elevated suicide risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bartoli, Crocamo et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive Symptoms: Cognitive impairments affecting attention, memory, and executive functions often persist during euthymia (Hussain, Suraweera et al. 2026).
text.formatted: Cognitive Symptoms: Cognitive impairments affecting attention, memory, and executive functions often persist during euthymia <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hussain, Suraweera et al. 2026</ref>).

text.text: These reflect the same neural disruptions producing mood symptoms (e.g., prefrontal dysfunction, hippocampal abnormalities).
Understanding cognitive difficulties as core features rather than mood byproducts reduces self-blame.
Understanding what drives bipolar disorder at the biological level gives patients a coherent account of why symptoms emerge and recur, rather than a list of unrelated facts.

The mechanisms below (i.e., neurotransmitter dysregulation, inflammation, circadian disruption, and kindling) interact and reinforce one another, and each offers a natural entry point for explaining why a specific treatment or lifestyle change matters.
Neurotransmitter Systems: Dopamine shows state-dependent alterations with hyperactivity during mania and hypoactivity during depression (Trouillas, Claustrat et al. 2025).
text.formatted: Neurotransmitter Systems: Dopamine shows state-dependent alterations with hyperactivity during mania and hypoactivity during depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Trouillas, Claustrat et al. 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Serotonin dysfunction contributes to impulsivity and depressive symptoms.
Norepinephrine regulates arousal, elevated during mania and reduced during depression.
For NIPE, neurotransmitters can be explained as chemical messengers enabling brain cell communication: when these systems become imbalanced, symptoms emerge.
Inflammation in BD involves elevated inflammatory markers during acute episodes (Fiori, Lombardo et al. 2026).
text.formatted: Inflammation in BD involves elevated inflammatory markers during acute episodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fiori, Lombardo et al. 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroinflammation may disrupt neural signaling, impair neuroplasticity, and damage cellular components.

Factors known to influence course also affect inflammation: stress increases it, while exercise, sleep, and healthy diet reduce it, providing a mechanistic explanation for lifestyle intervention benefits.
Circadian Biology: Humans evolved to live synchronized with 24-hour lightdark cycles.
In BD, clock systems become dysregulated; and sleep architecture is disrupted during both depressive and manic episodes (Geoffroy and Maruani 2025, Fiori, Lombardo et al. 2026).
text.formatted: In BD, clock systems become dysregulated; and sleep architecture is disrupted during both depressive and manic episodes <ref type="bibr">(Geoffroy and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maruani 2025, Fiori, Lombardo et al. 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Even during euthymia, sleep abnormalities are present in BD.
NIPE should emphasize that maintaining regular sleep-wake schedules is neurobiologically necessary for mood stability.
Kindling Processes: Each mood episode may produce neuroplastic changes increasing future vulnerability (Post 2007).
text.formatted: Kindling Processes: Each mood episode may produce neuroplastic changes increasing future vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Post 2007</ref>).

text.text: This has critical implications: early intervention becomes especially important because preventing episodes may prevent progressive neural changes.

Explaining risk and treatment mechanisms together helps patients see that vulnerability is not destiny: the same genetic and stress-related pathways that increase risk are also the targets treatment, including lithium, works to correct.  (Ochsner and Gross 2005).

text.text: Understanding that thoughts during episodes are products of altered neural processing rather than accurate reality creates psychological distance (e.g., "this is the illness talking" rather than "I am worthless").
Prospective Thinking: Developing individualized strategies, including prodromal symptoms, triggers, and tools to use if/when symptoms start to emerge, engages future-oriented cognition systems.
Creating relapse prevention plans during euthymia allows prefrontal executive functions to guide future behavior, even when compromised during episodes.

Because circadian disruption is both a trigger and a consequence of mood episodes, interventions that stabilize daily rhythms address the illness at its mechanistic root rather than only managing symptoms after they appear.
Social Rhythm Regularity: Regular mealtimes, exercise timing, and social interactions influence circadian systems.
IPSRT emphasizes social rhythm regularity based on evidence that social rhythms entrain biological rhythms (Frank 2007).

text.text: Maintaining regularity may be challenging during transitions, but understanding its neurobiological importance motivates routine preservation.

Rezapour, Berry, Cullum, and colleagues (2026) identify seven structural elements that determine how effectively NIPE content is processed and retained: salience, trustworthiness, intensity, repetition, motivation, multi-media delivery, and interaction.
The delivery considerations below for bipolar disorder instantiate these elements within a population defined by state-dependent cognitive function.
Timing decisions primarily govern intensity and motivation, presenting content when cognitive load can be tolerated and when the reward system is not already destabilized by mood state.
Phenotype-based personalization governs salience, ensuring content is self-relevant to the individual's specific illness course.
Multimodal and digital delivery address multi-media delivery and interaction, while family involvement extends trustworthiness beyond the individual to the caregiving system.
During acute manic episodes, impaired judgment, distractibility, and diminished illness awareness preclude meaningful engagement with educational content.
During severe depression, cognitive slowing and impaired concentration compromise information processing.
NIPE delivery should ideally occur during euthymic periods when cognitive function and insight are optimally available.
A staged approach aligns content with illness phases.
Upon diagnosis, basic information about illness and treatment is appropriate.
Following acute episode resolution represents an ideal window for comprehensive NIPE, as motivation is high due to recent episode, but mood stability allows effective processing.
During euthymia, NIPE can focus on advanced topics including relapse prevention.
Studies have shown that digital phenotyping can be done during any time of the illness, including active episodes (Ortiz, Park et al. 2023).

Mechanisms of NIPE Efficacy in BD NIPE may improve outcomes through multiple mechanisms: -Mechanistic understanding creates more robust illness awareness, less vulnerable to mood-state distortion (e.g., "when sleep drops below 5 hours for three nights, mood regulation systems destabilize" provides an objective framework resistant to cognitive biases and helps to identify tools needed to modify behavior).

-Reducing negative attitudes about psychiatric illness and self-deprecation, positioning BD as a brain-based medical condition comparable to diabetes rather than a character flaw (Sarı, Şengün İnan et al. 2025).
text.formatted: -Reducing negative attitudes about psychiatric illness and self-deprecation, positioning BD as a brain-based medical condition comparable to diabetes rather than a character flaw <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Sarı, Şengün İnan et al. 2025</ref>).

text.text: -Improving adherence through mechanistic rationale extends beyond symptom suppression.
For instance, understanding that lithium promotes neuroplasticity and protects neurons can motivate sustained use.
For individuals questioning medication need during wellness, explaining that euthymia reflects successful treatment is valuable.
-Transforming episodes from mysterious events to understandable phenomena with identifiable triggers and prodromal signs builds agency.
Knowledge enables better understanding of triggers, which enables preparation.
However, NIPE must balance agency emphasis with recognition that despite best efforts, episodes sometimes occur.
At the same time, understanding effective treatments exist reduces catastrophic fears about episode consequences.
-Fostering realistic expectations, which involves providing accurate information about illness course.
Neuroplasticity content supports optimism (e.g., recovery is possible, treatments promote beneficial brain changes).
However, NIPE should acknowledge BD is a chronic illness that requires ongoing management.
This balanced approach promotes sustained engagement necessary for long-term recovery.

text.text: Genetic and Epigenetic Factors: BD has strong genetic component (heritability 60-85%), but genes influence vulnerability rather than deterministically causing illness (O'Connell, Koromina et al.
Epigenetics (i.e., changes in gene expression) bridges genetic vulnerability and environmental influences.
For instance, substance use can produce epigenetic modifications altering brain function (Post 2016).
Importantly, epigenetic changes are potentially reversible, explaining how interventions modify illness course.
Stress and HPA Axis: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis mediates stress responses through cortisol secretion.
Chronic stress produces sustained activation with elevated cortisol, damaging the hippocampus, impairing neuroplasticity, and disrupting sleep (Krasner, Ong et al.
Stressful events frequently precede mood episodes, suggesting stress triggers neural cascades leading to destabilization.
Lithium's Neuroprotective Effects: Lithium increases gray matter volume in prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, promotes hippocampal neurogenesis, and enhances BDNF expression (Machado-Vieira 2018).
It modulates intracellular signaling affecting circadian rhythms and cellular resilience; and demonstrates anti-inflammatory properties.
NIPE should emphasize lithium is not merely suppressing symptoms but actively supporting brain health.Psychotherapy: Effective psychotherapy produces measurable brain changes.

text.text: Bipolar-Specific Brain Strategies 4.1 Cognitive Strategies Each of the following strategies works by making a specific neural process (e.g., self-monitoring, cognitive appraisal, future planning) available to deliberate use rather than leaving it automatic during mood episodes.
Mood Monitoring: Tracking multiple dimensions (e.g., mood, energy levels, sleep, anxiety, irritability) reflects that mood states involve complex neural system configurations.
NIPE should explain that monitoring makes implicit neural states explicit, and available to prefrontal cortex regulation.
It also helps patients to associate certain behaviors (e.g., exercise) with improvements in mood and energy; and others (e.g., drinking alcohol) with alterations in sleep.
Cognitive Restructuring: Mood episodes involve cognitive biases aligning with mood state.
During depression, negative biases produce overgeneralizing and catastrophizing; during hypomania, positive biases may produce overconfidence.
Cognitive restructuring engages prefrontal regions to reappraise emotional stimuli and modulate limbic reactivity
Hygiene as Neural Stabilization: Consistent sleep-wake times entrain the suprachiasmatic nucleus, strengthening circadian rhythms (McCarthy, Gottlieb et al.

Sleep environment influences sleep architecture quality: darkness promotes melatonin, cool temperature supports natural temperature drop, minimal noise protects slow-wave and REM sleep essential for neuroplasticity and emotional processing.
Pre-sleep routines signal the brain to initiate sleep processes.
Light Exposure: Morning bright light therapy (~10,000 lux for 30 minutes) suppresses melatonin, increases alertness, and entrains circadian rhythms (McCarthy, Gottlieb et al.
Blue-light blocking in evening protects melatonin secretion.
Understanding these mechanisms helps informed decisions about light exposure.

Personalization and Delivery Comorbidity: BD frequently co-occurs with anxiety disorders, ADHD, and substance use disorders (McElroy, Altshuler et al.
Comorbidity requires adapted content addressing shared neural circuits, bidirectional relationships, and integrated treatments.
Multi-Modal Delivery: Individual NIPE allows personalization, while group formats offer efficiency and therapeutic mechanisms including universality and peer learning.
Hybrid approaches combining group core content with individual sessions addressing personal factors optimize both.
Digital platforms enable selfpaced learning with multimedia features enhancing engagement (Saleem, Kühne et al.

Adaptive digital platforms represent a natural extension of this principle for bipolar disorder specifically: an implementation that adjusts content complexity and pacing based on a patient's current mood state and cognitive load, rather than delivering fixed content regardless of episode phase, would directly address the state-dependent variability in insight and processing capacity described in Section 5.1.
NIPE should integrate with evidence-based therapies (e.g., enriching CBT with neuroscience-based explanations of cognitive biases, framing IPSRT interventions within circadian-informed neuroscience).
Providing family members with neuroscience-informed education is also important to reduce blame.

Critical research gaps include a lack of RCTs comparing neuroscience-informed versus standard psychoeducation; a lack of research identifying which NIPE components are most effective; uncharacterized individual differences in responsiveness; a lack of studies on delivery parameters; and insufficient longterm outcome data.

Future strategies should include precision medicine approaches, involving phenotype-based personalization, tailoring content to clinical presentations, biomarker-informed NIPE incorporating neuroimaging or genetic findings, learning style adaptation, and cultural adaptation.

For bipolar disorder specifically, this points toward protocols differentiated by illness phenotype and course: distinct content sequencing for bipolar I versus bipolar II, for rapid cycling versus classic episodic presentations, and for early-course versus long-established illness, paired with digital phenotyping data to time content delivery to windows of highest receptivity, such as shortly after acute episode resolution.

Research priorities include RCTs comparing NIPE with standard psychoeducation, with adequate power to detect clinically meaningful effects on relapse rates and functioning; mediation analyses testing hypothesized mechanisms; moderator analyses examining individual differences; implementation science examining real-world delivery barriers and strategies; and qualitative research exploring individual experiences to inform refinement.

Conclusion Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation represents a promising evolution of traditional psychoeducational approaches for BD, grounded in contemporary understanding of neural circuitry, neuroplasticity, autonomic function, and neurochemistry.

The neuroscience foundation is robust: prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction, reward processing abnormalities oscillating across mood states, circadian rhythm disruptions destabilizing neural function, and autonomic dysregulation reflected in altered HRV patterns.

Understanding neuroplasticity mechanisms, both maladaptive changes contributing to progression and adaptive changes supporting recovery, provides framework for explaining treatment effects and motivating sustained management.
NIPE content should address diagnosis, pathogenesis, risk factors, treatment mechanisms, prognosis, and prevention.
Neuroscience principles can be translated into accessible language and meaningful metaphors conveying mechanistic understanding without requiring technical expertise.
Timing considerations are critical given state-dependent cognitive function and insight variations.
Euthymic phases represent optimal windows for comprehensive delivery.
Multi-modal delivery through individual sessions, groups, and digital platforms maximizes accessibility.
Family involvement creates shared understanding, though must balance with individual autonomy.

Efficacy mechanisms likely involve enhancing metacognitive awareness through mechanistic understanding; reducing negative attitudes and bias through biological explanations emphasizing neuroplasticity; improving adherence by clarifying medication mechanisms; building agency through knowledge; fostering realistic expectations; and reducing anxiety by transforming unpredictable episodes into understandable phenomena.

While empirical evidence specifically evaluating NIPE for BD remains limited, promising directions include integrating digital health technologies for real-time monitoring, developing precision medicine approaches that personalize content to phenotype and biomarkers, conducting rigorous RCTs with mediation and moderation analyses, implementing qualitative research, and pursuing implementation science to enable real-world translation.

NIPE transforms BD from an unpredictable, complex disorder into an understandable brain-based condition with identifiable mechanisms, measurable early warning signals, and actionable intervention strategies, thus empowering individuals to move from passive symptom endurance to active, informed selfmanagement grounded in contemporary understanding of neural circuitry, neuroplasticity, and autonomic function.
By effectively providing mechanistic knowledge about BD, NIPE can enhance illness awareness, treatment adherence, and self-efficacy, and improve clinical outcomes.
